ui.airway.cormack.about: The Cormack–Lehane grade, described in 1984, records the view obtained at direct laryngoscopy; it is not a predictive test but a description of what actually happened. In Grade 1 the glottis is fully seen, in Grade 2 partly, in Grade 3 only the epiglottis, and in Grade 4 no laryngeal structure is visible. In the modification proposed by Cook in 2000, Grade 2 is split into 2a, where the posterior cords are visible, and 2b, where only the arytenoids are seen; 2b and above are associated with meaningful difficulty. Grade 3 is split into 3a, where the epiglottis can be lifted, and 3b, where it cannot. Recording the view in the anesthetic chart together with any external laryngeal manipulation, use of a bougie and the blade used is the single most valuable piece of information for that patient's next airway.
ui.airway.cormack.band.difficult.detail: Grade 3–4: intubation by direct laryngoscopy fails in most cases. Move to videolaryngoscopy, a fibreoptic technique and the difficult airway algorithm; avoid repeated attempts.
ui.airway.cormack.band.difficult.title: Difficult view
ui.airway.cormack.band.easy.title: Easy view
ui.airway.cormack.band.restricted.detail: Grade 2b: the rate of difficult intubation rises markedly. Consider a bougie, a videolaryngoscope or external laryngeal manipulation (BURP).
ui.airway.cormack.band.restricted.title: Restricted view
ui.airway.cormack.hint.grade: Grade the best view obtained with optimal manoeuvres
ui.airway.cormack.name: Cormack-Lehane
ui.airway.cormack.note1: Grade the best view achieved with optimal positioning, external manipulation and an appropriate blade size.
ui.airway.cormack.note2: The view with a videolaryngoscope can be better than at direct laryngoscopy; record which device was used.
ui.airway.cormack.note3: The POGO score (percentage of glottic opening) is a complementary alternative.
ui.airway.cormack.note4: A grade 3–4 finding should be told to the patient and entered in the record.
ui.airway.cormack.optionDetail.g1: The whole glottic opening is visible.
ui.airway.cormack.optionDetail.g2a: Part of the glottis is visible; the anterior commissure is not.
ui.airway.cormack.optionDetail.g2b: Only the arytenoids or the most posterior part of the cords are visible.
ui.airway.cormack.optionDetail.g3: Only the epiglottis is visible (3a: liftable, 3b: not liftable).
ui.airway.cormack.optionDetail.g4: Not even the epiglottis is seen; only the soft palate is visible.
ui.airway.cormack.reference: Cormack & Lehane 1984; Cook 2000 (the modification adding the 2a/2b and 3a/3b subgroups).
ui.airway.cormack.subtitle: The structure seen at direct laryngoscopy
ui.airway.cormack.summary: This is not a prediction test: it grades the view obtained during laryngoscopy and should be documented.
ui.airway.lemon.about: LEMON is a memory aid developed for rapid airway assessment in the emergency department and pre-hospital care; the name comes from Look externally, Evaluate 3-3-2, Mallampati, Obstruction and Neck mobility. The external look covers trauma, a beard, a large tongue and a small jaw; the 3-3-2 rule asks for three fingers of mouth opening, three fingers between hyoid and mandible and two fingers between the thyroid notch and the floor of the mouth; Mallampati class, signs of upper airway obstruction and neck mobility follow. In the emergency department study by Reed and colleagues, the frequency of difficult laryngoscopy rose markedly as more items were marked. There is no validated cut-off; its purpose is to force a systematic screen in the seconds before a rapid sequence intubation and to make plan B explicit in advance.
ui.airway.lemon.band.high.detail: 3 or more items positive: a difficult airway is likely. The most experienced operator should intubate, the best device should be used on the first attempt and a front-of-neck plan should be ready.
ui.airway.lemon.band.high.title: High risk
ui.airway.lemon.band.low.detail: No item ticked: no known risk marker. Preparation and preoxygenation remain standard for emergency intubation.
ui.airway.lemon.band.low.title: No findings
ui.airway.lemon.band.moderate.detail: 1–2 items positive: difficult laryngoscopy becomes more likely. Keep a videolaryngoscope and a bougie at hand.
ui.airway.lemon.band.moderate.title: Limited risk
ui.airway.lemon.hint.interincisor: First step of the 3-3-2 rule (interincisor distance)
ui.airway.lemon.hint.look: Trauma, beard, short thick neck, marked obesity, abnormal facies, poor dentition
ui.airway.lemon.hint.neck: Cervical collar, trauma, ankylosing spondylitis, rheumatoid arthritis
ui.airway.lemon.hint.obstruction: Stridor, epiglottitis, peritonsillar abscess, tumour, neck hematoma
ui.airway.lemon.item.thyrofloor: Thyroid notch to floor of mouth < 2 fingers
ui.airway.lemon.name: LEMON assessment
ui.airway.lemon.note1: The 3-3-2 rule is assessed with the patient's own fingers.
ui.airway.lemon.note2: In an emergency not every item can be assessed; treating what you cannot assess as positive is the safe approach.
ui.airway.lemon.note3: LEMON screens for difficult laryngoscopy; difficult mask ventilation and difficult front-of-neck access must be judged separately.
ui.airway.lemon.note4: A positive screen does not mean postponing intubation; it changes the preparation and the choice of device.
ui.airway.lemon.reference: Reed MJ et al., Emerg Med J 2005;22:99-102. The original study used a 0–10 score with subcomponents.
ui.airway.lemon.subtitle: Emergency airway screening list · 0–7 items
ui.airway.lemon.summary: Look, Evaluate 3-3-2, Mallampati, Obstruction, Neck mobility. Every item ticked raises the risk; it is designed for rapid screening.
ui.airway.macocha.about: MACOCHA, developed and validated in a multicenter series by De Jong and colleagues in 2013, is the one score designed specifically to predict difficult intubation in the ICU, created because scores derived in the operating theatre perform poorly in the critically ill. Its seven items fall into three groups: patient factors (Mallampati III–IV, obstructive sleep apnea syndrome, reduced cervical mobility, mouth opening < 3 cm), pathology factors (coma, severe hypoxemia) and an operator factor (a non-anaesthetist operator). The total runs from 0 to 12, and 3 or more is positive for difficult intubation, with a negative predictive value close to 98% in the validation cohort. A low score is therefore reassuring, while a high score calls for an experienced operator, videolaryngoscopy, optimised preoxygenation and hemodynamic preparation.
ui.airway.macocha.band.high.detail: 3 points or more is positive for difficult intubation (sensitivity 73%, specificity 63%). Two operators, videolaryngoscopy, preoxygenation with noninvasive ventilation or high-flow nasal oxygen and haemodynamic preparation are advised.
ui.airway.macocha.band.high.title: High risk
ui.airway.macocha.band.low.detail: 0–2 points: difficult intubation is unlikely (negative predictive value 98%).
ui.airway.macocha.band.low.title: Low risk
ui.airway.macocha.name: MACOCHA score
ui.airway.macocha.note1: Intubation in the ICU carries a far higher complication rate than in the operating room; use a preparation checklist.
ui.airway.macocha.note2: Strengthen preoxygenation with high-flow nasal oxygen or noninvasive ventilation.
ui.airway.macocha.note3: Correct hypotension before intubation; have vasopressors and fluid ready.
ui.airway.macocha.note4: The score is validated only in critically ill patients; for operating room patients SARI or Wilson fit better.
ui.airway.macocha.reference: De Jong A et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2013;187:832-9.
ui.airway.macocha.subtitle: Predicting difficult intubation in the ICU · 0–12 points
ui.airway.macocha.summary: Seven items covering the patient, the pathology and the operator; 3 points or more is positive for difficult intubation.
ui.airway.mallampati.about: The Mallampati classification, described by Mallampati in 1985 and extended to four classes by Samsoon and Young, predicts difficult laryngoscopy from the pharyngeal structures visible on mouth opening. The patient sits with the head neutral, mouth fully open and tongue maximally protruded, without phonating: in Class I the soft palate, uvula and tonsillar pillars are seen, while in Class IV only the hard palate is visible. Classes III and IV are taken as a warning for difficult laryngoscopy. Used alone its predictive value is limited: sensitivity is moderate, the positive predictive value is low, and agreement between observers varies. It should therefore be read as part of a multivariable assessment, alongside thyromental distance, mouth opening, neck mobility and any history of difficult intubation.
ui.airway.mallampati.band.high.detail: Class III–IV is associated with difficult laryngoscopy. Sensitivity alone is limited (around 50%); interpret it together with thyromental distance, mouth opening and neck movement.
ui.airway.mallampati.band.high.title: High risk
ui.airway.mallampati.band.low.detail: Class I–II: difficult laryngoscopy is unlikely. Still weigh the other tests and the history.
ui.airway.mallampati.band.low.title: Low risk
ui.airway.mallampati.name: Modified Mallampati
ui.airway.mallampati.note1: Phonation (asking the patient to say "ah") artificially improves the class; assess in silence.
ui.airway.mallampati.note2: Assessment in the supine position can worsen the class by one grade; examine sitting where possible.
ui.airway.mallampati.note3: Inter-observer agreement is only moderate; repeat the assessment in doubtful cases.
ui.airway.mallampati.note4: Pregnancy, obesity and head and neck radiotherapy can worsen the class.
ui.airway.mallampati.optionDetail.i: Soft palate, the whole uvula, fauces and both pillars are visible.
ui.airway.mallampati.optionDetail.ii: Soft palate, uvula and fauces are visible; the pillars are not.
ui.airway.mallampati.optionDetail.iii: Soft palate and only the base of the uvula are visible.
ui.airway.mallampati.optionDetail.iv: The soft palate is not visible; only the hard palate can be seen.
ui.airway.mallampati.reference: Mallampati 1985; Samsoon & Young 1987 (the modified four-class version).
ui.airway.mallampati.subtitle: Oropharyngeal view classification
ui.airway.mallampati.summary: Assess with the patient sitting, head neutral, mouth opened fully and the tongue protruded as far as possible, without phonation.
ui.airway.sari.about: The El-Ganzouri risk index (SARI, Simplified Airway Risk Index) is a difficult-laryngoscopy score developed in 1996 in a prospective series of 10,507 patients, combining seven independent variables. They are mouth opening, thyromental distance, Mallampati class, neck movement, the ability to prognath, body weight and a history of difficult intubation, giving a total of 0–12. Four points or more is taken as high risk; at that threshold specificity is high and sensitivity moderate, so a low score reduces but does not remove the possibility of a difficult airway. Its advantage over tests based on a single examination finding is that it weights and combines several findings. A high score should prompt a change of plan — awake fiberoptic intubation or starting with videolaryngoscopy — and experienced help available in the room.
ui.airway.sari.band.high.detail: 4 points or more counts as high risk. Starting with a videolaryngoscope, having experienced help and considering awake intubation are appropriate.
ui.airway.sari.band.high.title: High risk
ui.airway.sari.band.low.detail: 0–3 points: difficult laryngoscopy is unlikely; a standard approach is appropriate.
ui.airway.sari.band.low.title: Low risk
ui.airway.sari.hint.prognathism: Ability to bring the lower incisors in front of the upper ones
ui.airway.sari.hint.thyromental: Thyroid notch to chin, head fully extended
ui.airway.sari.name: El-Ganzouri risk index
ui.airway.sari.note1: The index discriminates better than single tests and has entered preoperative forms in many centres.
ui.airway.sari.note2: A history of difficult intubation is the single strongest predictor; always ask for the old anesthetic records.
ui.airway.sari.note3: Thyromental distance varies with the patient's height; the height-to-thyromental ratio adds information.
ui.airway.sari.note4: A high score is not an absolute contraindication; it determines the equipment and the team you prepare.
ui.airway.sari.reference: El-Ganzouri AR et al., Anesth Analg 1996;82:1197-204.
ui.airway.sari.subtitle: Simplified airway risk index (SARI) · 0–12 points
ui.airway.sari.summary: Seven parameters; 4 points or more is taken as high risk for difficult laryngoscopy.
ui.airway.warn.documentation.message: Record the assessment and the Cormack-Lehane grade seen at laryngoscopy in the anesthetic chart; if a difficult airway is found, inform the patient and document it.
ui.airway.warn.documentation.title: Record and hand over
ui.airway.warn.plan.message: Keep the difficult airway trolley, a videolaryngoscope, a supraglottic airway and a bougie at hand; call an experienced second operator, extend preoxygenation, and consider awake intubation or a front-of-neck plan in advance.
ui.airway.warn.plan.title: Have plan B ready
ui.airway.warn.positive.message: {score}: {total} points, above the published threshold of {threshold}. Plan for a difficult intubation.
ui.airway.warn.positive.title: High risk of a difficult airway
ui.airway.warn.singleTest.message: Airway prediction tests have low sensitivity on their own. Combine several tests with the history (previous difficult intubation, obstructive sleep apnea, radiotherapy, neck surgery) and with the likelihood of difficult mask ventilation.
ui.airway.warn.singleTest.title: No single test is enough
ui.airway.wilson.about: The Wilson risk score, described by Wilson and colleagues in 1988, grades five anatomical and clinical variables from 0 to 2 to predict difficult laryngoscopy. The variables are body weight, head and neck movement, jaw movement, a receding mandible and buck teeth, giving a total of 0–10. In the original study a threshold of 2 points identified roughly 75% of difficult laryngoscopies while producing false positives in about 12% of patients. As a predictive instrument it remains weak to moderate; its real value is that it makes the airway examination systematic and forces attention onto several risk markers rather than one. A difficult airway plan should be ready in every patient, whatever the score.
ui.airway.wilson.band.high.detail: 2 points or more counts as positive for difficult laryngoscopy (sensitivity about 75%, specificity about 88% in the original study). The false-positive rate is high; interpret with the other tests.
ui.airway.wilson.band.high.title: At risk
ui.airway.wilson.band.low.title: Low risk
ui.airway.wilson.hint.jaw: Mouth opening (interincisor gap) and forward subluxation of the mandible
ui.airway.wilson.name: Wilson risk score
ui.airway.wilson.note1: The score was developed in 1988 for direct laryngoscopy; its predictive power is limited in the era of videolaryngoscopy.
ui.airway.wilson.note2: Obesity alone is associated more with difficult mask ventilation than with difficult intubation.
ui.airway.wilson.note3: Atlanto-occipital extension is markedly reduced by a cervical collar, ankylosing spondylitis and rheumatoid arthritis.
ui.airway.wilson.note4: The ability to protrude the mandible (upper lip bite test) is a meaningful indicator on its own.
ui.airway.wilson.reference: Wilson ME et al., Br J Anaesth 1988;61:211-6.
ui.airway.wilson.subtitle: Prediction of difficult laryngoscopy · 0–10 points
ui.airway.wilson.summary: Each of five parameters is graded 0–2. A total of 2 or more is a warning sign for difficult laryngoscopy.

ui.bg.about: This screen applies the classical Boston (physiological) approach, which works an arterial blood gas out in six steps. The pH first tells you whether there is acidemia or alkalemia; the direction of HCO₃ and PaCO₂ then identifies the primary disorder. The third step calculates the anion gap and corrects it for albumin — skip that in a critically ill patient and a high anion gap acidosis is easily missed. The fourth step tests whether compensation lies in the expected range: Winters' formula for metabolic acidosis, 0.7 × HCO₃ + 20 for metabolic alkalosis, and for respiratory disorders an expected HCO₃ that differs according to whether the problem is acute or chronic. Any value outside the expected range points to a second disorder. The fifth step uses the delta ratio to show whether a normal anion gap acidosis or a metabolic alkalosis accompanies a high anion gap acidosis. The sixth step assembles the findings into one statement and lists the differential headings. The advanced block offers two complementary methods: partitioned base excess splits the standard base excess into chloride, albumin, lactate and unmeasured-anion components, while the Stewart approach comes at the same question through the strong ion difference (SID) and strong ion gap (SIG). The screen never hides the raw values and always shows which rule produced each step; judgements that need clinical input, such as acute versus chronic, remain yours.
ui.bg.caption.beAlb: 0.25 × (42 − albumin g/L) · a positive value is the alkalinizing effect of hypoalbuminemia
ui.bg.caption.beCl: Na − Cl − 32 · a negative value is the hyperchloremic acidosis contribution
ui.bg.caption.beGap: SBE − (chloride + albumin + lactate components) · markedly negative means unmeasured anions
ui.bg.caption.beLac: 1 − lactate · a negative value is the lactic acidosis contribution
ui.bg.caption.sid: Normal 38–42 mEq/L · a low SID is acidogenic
ui.bg.caption.sig: AG − A⁻; A⁻ = albumin (g/L) × (0.123·pH − 0.631) + phosphate (mmol/L) × (0.309·pH − 0.469). Above 2 means unmeasured anions
ui.bg.case1.detail: 58 years old, cirrhosis, resuscitated with 0.9% NaCl. Na 134, Cl 108, HCO₃ 12.6, albumin 1.9 g/dL. The raw AG of 13.4 looks normal. Corrected AG = 13.4 + 2.5 × (4 − 1.9) = 18.7 → this really is a high anion gap acidosis.
ui.bg.case1.label: CASE 1
ui.bg.case1.title: HAGMA and the albumin trap
ui.bg.case2.detail: Corrected AG 25.5, HCO₃ 17.2, pH 7.39 (normal). Delta ratio = (25.5 − 12) / (24 − 17.2) = 1.99 → a metabolic alkalosis accompanies the HAGMA. The pH is misleadingly normal.
ui.bg.case2.label: CASE 2
ui.bg.case2.title: A mixed disorder found by the delta ratio
ui.bg.case3.detail: In 0.9% NaCl, Na = Cl = 154 → SID = 0, which is acidogenic. In a balanced crystalloid SID ≈ 38–40 → acid-base neutral, and preferable in large volumes.
ui.bg.case3.label: CASE 3
ui.bg.case3.title: Choosing a fluid by its SID
ui.bg.check4: Was the anion gap checked even though the pH was normal?
ui.bg.check5: Was the SID of the fluid being given considered?
ui.bg.etiology.hagma: High anion gap: lactate, ketoacidosis (diabetic, starvation, alcoholic), uremia, toxic alcohols (methanol, ethylene glycol), salicylate, propylene glycol, pyroglutamic acid.
ui.bg.etiology.lactate: Lactate {lactate} mmol/L — look for tissue hypoperfusion, sepsis, mesenteric ischemia, drugs (metformin, linezolid, propofol) and liver failure.
ui.bg.etiology.metAlkalosis: Metabolic alkalosis: vomiting and nasogastric drainage, diuretics, hypokalemia, hypovolemia, excess bicarbonate or citrate load, mineralocorticoid excess.
ui.bg.etiology.nagma: Normal anion gap acidosis: diarrhea, large volumes of 0.9% NaCl, renal tubular acidosis, ureteral diversion, early renal failure, acetazolamide. The urinary anion gap discriminates.
ui.bg.etiology.respAcidosis: Respiratory acidosis: hypoventilation, sedation, neuromuscular weakness, COPD exacerbation, inadequate ventilator settings, air trapping.
ui.bg.etiology.respAlkalosis: Respiratory alkalosis: pain, anxiety, fever, sepsis, hypoxemia, pulmonary embolism, liver failure, a central cause, over-ventilation.

ui.bg.hint.chloride: Needed for the anion gap and SID
ui.bg.hint.chronicity: Changes the compensation formula only when the primary disorder is respiratory

ui.bg.name: Arterial blood gas analysis
ui.bg.note1: Normal ranges: pH 7.35–7.45 · PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg · HCO₃ 22–26 mEq/L · BE ±2.3 · AG 8–12 · SID 38–42 · SIG 0–2.
ui.bg.note2: Compensation formulas: in metabolic acidosis PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃ + 8 ± 2; in metabolic alkalosis PaCO₂ = 0.7 × HCO₃ + 20 ± 5.
ui.bg.note3: Expected change in HCO₃ per 10 mmHg of PaCO₂ in respiratory disorders: acute acidosis +1, chronic acidosis +3.5–4, acute alkalosis −2, chronic alkalosis −5.
ui.bg.note4: Compensation never returns the pH fully to normal (chronic respiratory alkalosis is a partial exception); a perfectly normal pH suggests two disorders offsetting each other.
ui.bg.note5: SIG is calculated here in the simplified form AG − A⁻; the weak-acid charge (A⁻) uses the pH-dependent equations of Figge et al. (1992), giving coefficients of about 0.28 and 1.8 at pH 7.40. Because K⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ and lactate are not included, it can differ from the full Stewart–Figge SIG (SIDa − SIDe). Enter phosphate in mmol/L.
ui.bg.note6: This screen does not assess oxygenation (P/F ratio, A-a gradient); it works out the acid-base picture only.
ui.bg.primary.indeterminate: Indeterminate — the values do not fit a simple pattern
ui.bg.reference: Boston approach: Winters RW et al.; Albert MS et al., Ann Intern Med 1967;66:312-22. Albumin correction: Figge J et al., Crit Care Med 1998;26:1807-10. Partitioned BE: Story DA et al., Br J Anaesth 2004;92:54-60. Stewart approach: Stewart PA, Can J Physiol Pharmacol 1983;61:1444-61; Figge J et al., J Lab Clin Med 1992;120:713-9.

ui.bg.warn.albuminTrap.message: The raw anion gap of {ag} looks normal, but the albumin-corrected value is {agk}. Without the correction this high anion gap acidosis would have been missed.
ui.bg.warn.albuminTrap.title: The albumin trap
ui.bg.warn.chronicity.message: The duration of a respiratory disorder cannot be read from the blood gas, yet it determines the compensation formula. The wrong choice can invent a metabolic disorder that is not there.
ui.bg.warn.chronicity.title: Acute or chronic is your judgement
ui.bg.warn.compensationLimit.message: At this level respiratory compensation has reached its physiological limit; if respiratory fatigue sets in the pH will fall quickly. Assess the need for ventilatory support early.
ui.bg.warn.compensationLimit.title: HCO₃ < 6 mEq/L — compensation at its limit
ui.bg.warn.deltaBorderline.message: The table reads values above 2.0 as metabolic alkalosis, but 1.8–2.0 sits on the boundary and a coexisting metabolic alkalosis cannot be excluded. In the worked case on the pocket card a ratio of 1.99 is read as HAGMA plus metabolic alkalosis; check the clinical picture (vomiting, diuretics, nasogastric drainage).
ui.bg.warn.deltaBorderline.title: Delta ratio close to the boundary ({ratio})
ui.bg.warn.interpretation.message: Compensation formulas are estimates derived in particular populations and carry ± ranges. This screen never hides the raw values; read the result together with the clinical picture, the history and the laboratory.
ui.bg.warn.interpretation.title: An interpretation is not a diagnosis
ui.bg.warn.normalPh.message: A normal pH does not mean there is no disorder. Two disorders that offset each other leave the pH normal, which is why the anion gap and delta ratio should always be calculated.
ui.bg.warn.normalPh.title: The pH is normal but the picture is not
ui.bg.warn.severeAcidemia.message: Myocardial contractility falls, the response to catecholamines is blunted and the risk of arrhythmia rises. Treating the cause takes priority; bicarbonate is not routinely recommended.
ui.bg.warn.severeAcidemia.title: Severe acidemia (pH < 7.10)
ui.bg.warn.severeAlkalemia.message: Cerebral vasoconstriction, arrhythmia, a fall in ionized calcium and respiratory depression may follow. Correct chloride and potassium deficits and look for the cause.
ui.bg.warn.severeAlkalemia.title: Severe alkalemia (pH ≥ 7.60)
ui.bg.warn.sig.message: A SIG above 2 suggests anions that the routine panel does not show (intermediates of sepsis, toxins, ketoacids). The value is sensitive to the formula used and to the units of phosphate.
ui.bg.warn.sig.title: SIG {sig} mmol/L — unmeasured anion load

ui.electro.aniongap.about: The anion gap is a simple but powerful tool for showing the accumulation of unmeasured anions: Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). Used alone in intensive care it misleads, because albumin is the most important unmeasured anion and is frequently low in the critically ill; each 1 g/dL fall in albumin lowers the anion gap by about 2.5 mmol/L. A normal anion gap read without that correction can therefore hide an established lactic acidosis. The second step is the delta ratio: the rise in anion gap relative to the fall in bicarbonate shows whether a second acid-base disorder accompanies the picture — values between 1 and 2 indicate pure high anion gap acidosis, below 0.4 the predominance of a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) acidosis, and above 2 a coexisting metabolic alkalosis or chronic respiratory acidosis. The third step is Winter's formula: expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2. If the measured PaCO₂ falls outside that range the respiratory response is either inadequate or an independent respiratory disorder has been added. Together the three steps are enough to unpick a multi-component acid-base picture from a single blood gas.
ui.electro.aniongap.hint.albumin: A low albumin masks the anion gap
ui.electro.aniongap.hint.bicarbonate: HCO₃⁻ from the blood gas or serum total CO₂
ui.electro.aniongap.hint.paco2: Compared with the value expected from Winter's formula
ui.electro.aniongap.name: Anion gap panel
ui.electro.aniongap.note1: Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). The version that includes potassium has a normal range about 4 mmol/L higher; this screen uses the version without potassium.
ui.electro.aniongap.note2: Corrected anion gap = raw AG + 2.5 × (4 − albumin g/dL). In the critically ill this correction should be routine.
ui.electro.aniongap.note3: Delta ratio = (corrected AG − 12) / (24 − HCO₃⁻). Bands: < 0.4 NAGMA · 0.4–0.8 mixed · 0.8–2.0 pure HAGMA · > 2.0 HAGMA plus alkalosis.
ui.electro.aniongap.note4: Common causes of a high anion gap acidosis are lactate, ketoacidosis, uremia, toxic alcohols and salicylate. Measuring lactate and ketones separates them.
ui.electro.aniongap.note5: This screen does not calculate an osmolar gap; where toxic alcohol is suspected, request a measured osmolality separately.
ui.electro.aniongap.reference: Figge J et al., Crit Care Med 1998;26:1807-10 (albumin correction). Albert MS et al., Ann Intern Med 1967;66:312-22 (Winter's formula).

ui.electro.aniongap.summary: Assesses the type of metabolic acidosis, any second disorder alongside it, and the adequacy of the respiratory response on one screen.
ui.electro.aniongap.verdict.alkalosis: Delta ratio > 2: consider a coexisting metabolic alkalosis or chronic respiratory acidosis.

ui.electro.aniongap.verdict.mixed: Delta ratio 0.4–0.8: high and normal anion gap acidosis together.
ui.electro.aniongap.verdict.nagma: Delta ratio < 0.4: predominantly normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) acidosis.
ui.electro.aniongap.verdict.normalGap: The anion gap is normal. Any acidosis present is of the normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) type.
ui.electro.aniongap.verdict.pureAgma: Delta ratio 0.8–2.0: pure high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

ui.electro.aniongap.warn.albumin.title: Low albumin — correction is essential

ui.electro.corrections.about: This screen corrects the two commonest laboratory illusions in intensive care. The first is sodium in hyperglycemia: a high glucose osmotically draws water out of cells and dilutes the serum sodium. This is a genuine dilutional hyponatremia rather than a pseudohyponatremia, but it does not reflect the patient's total body water. The classical correction adds 1.6 mmol/L for every 100 mg/dL rise in glucose; Hillier's experimental study showed that 2.4 is closer to reality once glucose passes 400 mg/dL. A high corrected sodium signals a real free water deficit that will emerge as insulin brings the glucose down, and following that trend matters during treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis. The second is total calcium: about half of calcium is carried bound to albumin, so in hypoalbuminemia the total calcium reads low while the biologically active ionized fraction may be normal. Payne's albumin correction (measured Ca + 0.8 × (4 − albumin)) works well in outpatients but loses reliability in the critically ill because of acid-base shifts, citrate anticoagulation and rapid changes in albumin. Measuring ionized calcium on a blood gas is therefore always preferable in intensive care.
ui.electro.corrections.hint.factor: Sodium correction per 100 mg/dL rise in glucose
ui.electro.corrections.name: Corrected sodium and calcium
ui.electro.corrections.note2: Corrected calcium = measured Ca + 0.8 × (4 − albumin g/dL).
ui.electro.corrections.note3: The hyponatremia seen with hyperglycemia is osmotically real (dilutional), not pseudohyponatremia; pseudohyponatremia occurs with severe hyperlipidemia and hyperproteinemia.
ui.electro.corrections.note4: Track the corrected sodium while treating diabetic ketoacidosis; if it fails to rise as glucose falls, there is excess free water.
ui.electro.corrections.reference: Katz MA. N Engl J Med 1973;289:843-4 (factor 1.6). Hillier TA et al., Am J Med 1999;106:399-403 (factor 2.4). Payne RB et al., Br Med J 1973;4:643-6 (calcium).

ui.electro.corrections.summary: Shows the true sodium in hyperglycemia and the true calcium in hypoalbuminemia.

ui.electro.corrections.verdict.normal: The corrected sodium is within the normal range.

ui.electro.crystalloids.about: The choice of crystalloid has been debated in intensive care for years, and chloride sits at the centre of the argument. In 0.9% NaCl the sodium and chloride contents are equal at 154 mmol/L; because that chloride is about 1.5 times the plasma level, large volumes produce a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis and may cause renal vasoconstriction and a fall in glomerular filtration. Balanced solutions (Ringer's lactate, acetate-gluconate buffered solutions) bring the chloride closer to plasma and make up the missing anion with a buffer that the liver converts to bicarbonate. Large randomized trials looked for the clinical consequence of that difference: in the SMART trial balanced solutions were superior to 0.9% NaCl for a composite of death, new renal replacement therapy and persistent renal dysfunction, while the PLUS trial found no difference in 90-day mortality. Current practice generally favours balanced solutions for large volumes to avoid hyperchloremia, while staying with 0.9% NaCl in specific settings such as hyponatremia, hypochloremic alkalosis and traumatic brain injury. The values in the table are nominal contents; small differences exist between products and countries, so the product information of the fluid in hand takes precedence.

ui.electro.fena.about: The fractional excretion of sodium shows what percentage of the sodium filtered at the glomerulus is excreted in the urine, and so measures the kidney's effort to retain sodium. In prerenal azotemia the kidney is structurally intact and responds to hypoperfusion by reabsorbing sodium, driving FENa below 1%. In acute tubular necrosis the tubular cells are damaged and cannot reabsorb sodium, so FENa rises above 2%. The test's most important limitation is diuretic use: diuretics increase sodium excretion directly, so FENa rises even in a prerenal patient and the test becomes unusable. In that situation urea excretion is used instead, because urea is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule and is largely unaffected by loop diuretics; a FEUrea below 35% supports a prerenal cause. It should also be remembered that a low FENa does not always mean prerenal: in contrast nephropathy, rhabdomyolysis, early obstruction and the hepatorenal and cardiorenal syndromes, sodium retention continues despite structural injury. The test is meaningful only in the oliguric patient and should be read alongside the urine sediment and the clinical course rather than alone.
ui.electro.fena.name: FENa and FEUrea
ui.electro.fena.note1: FENa (%) = (urine Na × serum creatinine) / (serum Na × urine creatinine) × 100.
ui.electro.fena.note2: FEUrea (%) = (urine urea × serum creatinine) / (serum urea × urine creatinine) × 100.
ui.electro.fena.note3: Thresholds: FENa < 1% prerenal, > 2% intrinsic; FEUrea < 35% prerenal, > 50% intrinsic.
ui.electro.fena.note4: Take the samples at the same time; hours between the blood and urine sample make the result misleading.
ui.electro.fena.note5: The test discriminates only modestly; read it with the urine sediment (granular casts), renal ultrasound and the response to fluid.
ui.electro.fena.reference: Espinel CH. JAMA 1976;236:579-81 (FENa). Carvounis CP et al., Kidney Int 2002;62:2223-9 (FEUrea on diuretics).
ui.electro.fena.subtitle: Fractional excretion of sodium and urea
ui.electro.fena.summary: Helps separate a prerenal cause from intrinsic (tubular) injury in oliguric acute kidney injury.
ui.electro.fena.verdict.indeterminate: FENa 1–2%: not discriminating. Read it with FEUrea, the urine sediment and the clinical course.
ui.electro.fena.verdict.intrinsic: FENa above 2%: consistent with intrinsic injury (acute tubular necrosis).
ui.electro.fena.verdict.invalid: The calculation cannot be performed with these values; check the creatinine and sodium entries.
ui.electro.fena.verdict.prerenal: FENa below 1%: consistent with prerenal azotemia; the kidney is retaining sodium.
ui.electro.fena.warn.diuretic.message: Diuretics increase sodium excretion, so FENa rises even in a prerenal patient. Use FEUrea instead: values below 35% support a prerenal cause.

ui.electro.fluidbalance.about: Cumulative fluid overload is the positive fluid balance a patient has accumulated in intensive care, expressed against body weight: (cumulative balance in litres / admission weight in kilograms) × 100. Simple as the calculation is, it is one of the least regularly tracked measures in critical care. Observational studies and secondary analyses of large randomized trials have shown that a cumulative overload above 10% is associated with mortality, prolonged mechanical ventilation, raised intra-abdominal pressure and delayed recovery from acute kidney injury. Causality is debated — sicker patients both receive more fluid and do worse — but the evidence that a positive balance worsens outcomes has established an approach that divides fluid therapy into phases: resuscitation, optimization, stabilization and fluid removal. Once shock has resolved, the aim is not to maintain the positive balance but to actively reverse it. In practice the largest source of fluid is often not resuscitation boluses but the overlooked volumes of drug dilutions, continuous infusions and line flushes.
ui.electro.fluidbalance.hint.days: Period over which the balance was accumulated
ui.electro.fluidbalance.hint.intake: All fluids: infusions, drugs, feed, blood products
ui.electro.fluidbalance.hint.weight: Weight on admission to intensive care
ui.electro.fluidbalance.name: Cumulative fluid balance
ui.electro.fluidbalance.note1: Percent fluid overload = (cumulative balance in L / admission weight in kg) × 100.
ui.electro.fluidbalance.note2: The association is established but causality is debated: sicker patients both receive more fluid and do worse.
ui.electro.fluidbalance.note3: Drug dilutions, continuous infusions and line flushes are often missing from the chart, so true intake is higher than the recorded figure.
ui.electro.fluidbalance.note4: In acute kidney injury a positive balance dilutes creatinine and can make the stage look milder than it is.

ui.electro.hypernatremia.about: Hypernatremia is almost always the result of water loss or of being unable to reach water, and in intensive care it is common in the intubated, obtunded patient who cannot act on thirst. Treatment rests on two questions: how much water is missing, and how fast it should be given. The free water deficit is found by multiplying total body water by the ratio of current to target sodium: TBW × (current Na / target Na − 1). That figure covers only the missing water; ongoing urinary, gastrointestinal and insensible losses must be added, or the sodium will stubbornly stay high. The rule on speed depends on duration: in chronic hypernatremia lasting more than 48 hours the brain has osmotically adapted and giving water quickly can cause cerebral edema, so the fall is limited to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours. Where hypernatremia developed acutely that adaptation has not occurred and correction at up to 1 mmol/L per hour is safe. In the hypovolemic patient the order matters: stabilise the circulation with isotonic fluid first, then replace free water.

ui.electro.hyponatremia.about: The Adrogué–Madias formula estimates how many mmol/L one litre of a chosen infusion fluid will raise the serum sodium: (infusate sodium − serum sodium) / (total body water + 1). From this comes the volume needed to reach a 24-hour target and the hourly rate. The formula's value lies in setting the starting rate; the real safety lies in limiting the speed of correction. In chronic hyponatremia the brain has osmotically adapted, so rapid correction can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome; the rise over 24 hours is therefore capped at 8 mmol/L in the standard patient and 6 mmol/L where risk factors such as malnutrition, alcohol use disorder, hypokalemia or advanced liver disease are present. The formula's known weakness is that it ignores ongoing urinary losses: once hypovolemia is corrected and a water diuresis begins, sodium can rise far faster than predicted. It is therefore used alongside, not instead of, sodium measurement every 2–4 hours. With severe symptoms such as seizures or coma, do not wait for any calculation: give 150 mL of 3% NaCl over 20 minutes and repeat until the sodium has risen by 5 mmol/L.

ui.electro.kdigo.about: The KDIGO 2012 classification standardised the definition of acute kidney injury by merging the earlier RIFLE and AKIN criteria into one system. Any one of three criteria is enough for the diagnosis: a rise in creatinine of ≥ 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, a rise to ≥ 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for more than 6 hours. Staging is applied separately to the creatinine and urine output criteria and the patient takes whichever stage is higher; in practice the urine output criterion usually turns positive first, because creatinine is a late marker that takes hours to rise even after the glomerular filtration rate has halved. Starting renal replacement therapy means stage 3 regardless of the other values. The classification has two known weaknesses: where the baseline creatinine is unknown, using the admission value understates the stage in a patient who arrives already injured, and a positive fluid balance produces the same error by diluting creatinine. The stage does not dictate treatment, but as it rises so do mortality and the risk of chronic kidney disease; at every stage the shared approach is to stop nephrotoxic exposure, optimize perfusion and adjust drug doses.

ui.electro.potassium.about: Hypokalemia is the commonest electrolyte disturbance in intensive care and its danger lies mostly in arrhythmia. Serum potassium reflects only a small part of total body potassium — 98% of it is intracellular — so the deficit can only be estimated roughly from the serum value: each 1 mmol/L fall corresponds to about 200–400 mmol. In replacement, rate and concentration matter more than the total amount. Potassium given peripherally causes pain and phlebitis at concentrations above 40 mmol/L; established practice is not to exceed 10 mmol per hour peripherally, or 20 mmol per hour through a central line with continuous ECG monitoring. Potassium is never given as a bolus under any circumstances. The second common error is forgetting magnesium: hypomagnesemia sustains renal potassium wasting and creates hypokalemia refractory to replacement, so the two are measured and replaced together. Where alkalosis, insulin or beta-agonists have shifted potassium into cells there may be no true deficit at all; high-dose replacement given without making that distinction produces hyperkalemia once the shift resolves.

ui.sepsis.apache2.about: APACHE II, published by Knaus and colleagues in 1985, is the classic severity-of-illness system for intensive care patients. Twelve physiological variables taken as the worst values in the first 24 hours of admission are combined with a points allowance for age and one for chronic organ insufficiency or immunocompromise, giving a total of 0–71. Predicted hospital mortality rises steeply with the score: in the original series it was around 4% at 0–4 points and approached 85% above 35 points. A true mortality estimate also requires the coefficient for the patient's admission diagnostic category and whether surgery was emergency, entered into a regression equation; this screen reports the raw score and the published mortality bands. Its most important limitation is that it was designed to compare severity of illness between groups: a decision to limit treatment or to refuse ICU admission for an individual patient must not rest on an APACHE II score.

ui.sepsis.camicu.about: CAM-ICU is the adaptation of the Confusion Assessment Method for detecting delirium at the bedside in an intensive care patient who cannot speak. The assessment has two steps: sedation is first measured with the RASS, and if the patient is at RASS −4 or −5 (no response to voice) the test cannot be applied and is recorded as unable to assess. In a responsive patient four features are sought: acute onset or fluctuating course, inattention, altered level of consciousness and disorganized thinking. Delirium requires features 1 and 2 together with at least one of features 3 or 4 — no points are added up, a logical algorithm decides. Validation studies reported sensitivity and specificity above 90% with high agreement between raters. Because delirium in the ICU is associated with prolonged ventilation, higher mortality and long-term cognitive impairment, the PADIS 2018 guideline recommends routine screening every shift; without screening most cases, especially hypoactive delirium, go unnoticed.
ui.sepsis.camicu.band.negative.detail: CAM-ICU negative. Repeat screening at least once per shift and whenever mental status changes.
ui.sepsis.camicu.band.negative.title: No delirium
ui.sepsis.camicu.band.positive.detail: Features 1 and 2 with feature 3 or 4. Look for a cause and apply the ABCDEF bundle.
ui.sepsis.camicu.band.positive.title: Delirium present
ui.sepsis.camicu.band.unassessable.detail: RASS −4 / −5. Reassess once the patient responds to verbal stimulation.
ui.sepsis.camicu.band.unassessable.title: Unable to assess
ui.sepsis.camicu.hint.acuteChange: Is mental status acutely changed from baseline, or has it fluctuated in the past 24 hours?
ui.sepsis.camicu.hint.consciousness: Any RASS other than 0 (not alert and calm) is positive
ui.sepsis.camicu.hint.disorganized: Four yes/no questions and one command; 2 or more errors is positive
ui.sepsis.camicu.hint.inattention: Letter attention test: the patient squeezes on hearing "A" in ten letters; 3 or more errors is positive
ui.sepsis.camicu.hint.sedation: Measure RASS first. Assessment is not possible at RASS −4 or −5
ui.sepsis.camicu.item.acuteChange: Feature 1 · Acute onset or fluctuating course
ui.sepsis.camicu.name: CAM-ICU
ui.sepsis.camicu.note1: The order matters: RASS first, then CAM-ICU. At RASS −4/−5 no assessment is made and it is recorded as "UTA".
ui.sepsis.camicu.note2: The commonest form of delirium is hypoactive; because there is no agitation it is missed unless screening is routine.
ui.sepsis.camicu.note3: A positive result is not in itself a reason to start an antipsychotic; the PADIS 2018 guideline does not recommend routine haloperidol or atypical antipsychotics to treat delirium.
ui.sepsis.camicu.note4: Look for reversible causes first: hypoxia, hypotension, infection, electrolyte and glucose disturbance, pain, urinary retention, drug effects and withdrawal.
ui.sepsis.camicu.note5: Glasses and hearing aids, early mobilization, sleep hygiene, reorientation and minimal sedation are the basis of both prevention and treatment.
ui.sepsis.camicu.reference: Ely EW et al. JAMA 2001;286:2703-10 and Crit Care Med 2001;29:1370-9. One of the two tools recommended in the SCCM PADIS 2018 guideline.
ui.sepsis.camicu.subtitle: Delirium assessment in the ICU · algorithm
ui.sepsis.camicu.summary: Four features. Delirium is present when features 1 and 2 are both there and at least one of features 3 or 4 accompanies them. It works in the intubated patient who cannot speak.
ui.sepsis.camicu.warn.positive.message: Delirium is present. Look for a cause (infection, hypoxia, metabolic disturbance, drugs, pain, sleep deprivation), review deliriogenic medication and apply the ABCDEF bundle. Antipsychotics are not routine treatment.
ui.sepsis.camicu.warn.positive.title: CAM-ICU positive
ui.sepsis.camicu.warn.unassessable.message: CAM-ICU cannot be performed at RASS −4 or −5. Review the sedation target and reassess once the patient responds to voice.
ui.sepsis.camicu.warn.unassessable.title: Deeply sedated — cannot be assessed
ui.sepsis.cfs.about: The Clinical Frailty Scale, developed by Rockwood and colleagues within the Canadian Study of Health and Aging, grades frailty on nine levels from 1 to 9. It is not a questionnaire but a holistic judgement based on function, mobility, cognition and dependency in activities of daily living, and it is scored on the patient's baseline about two weeks before the acute illness rather than on how they look during it. Its importance in intensive care comes from the fact that chronological age alone is a poor predictor of outcome: of two patients of the same age, the frail one has markedly higher mortality and a greater risk of prolonged ventilation and dependency after discharge. In the multicentre study by Bagshaw and colleagues, critically ill patients with a CFS of 5 or more had significantly higher hospital mortality and worse outcomes at one year. The scale was developed for people over 65 and does not apply to younger patients or to stable single-organ disability; nor can it by itself justify refusing intensive care or limiting treatment — it is one part of a goals-of-care conversation with the patient and family.
ui.sepsis.cfs.band.fit.detail: Fit, or medical problems well controlled. Relatively better prospects of recovery after intensive care.
ui.sepsis.cfs.band.fit.title: 1–3 · not frail
ui.sepsis.cfs.band.frail.detail: Above the frailty threshold (≥ 5). ICU series show a clear rise in mortality, dependency and loss of quality of life.
ui.sepsis.cfs.band.frail.title: 5–6 · mild to moderate frailty
ui.sepsis.cfs.band.severe.detail: High risk of death and permanent dependency. Goals of care should be discussed openly with the patient and family.
ui.sepsis.cfs.band.severe.title: 7–9 · severe frailty
ui.sepsis.cfs.band.vulnerable.detail: Not yet dependent but with reduced reserve; at risk of rapid deterioration during acute illness.
ui.sepsis.cfs.band.vulnerable.title: 4 · very mild frailty
ui.sepsis.cfs.hint.level: Judge the baseline state roughly two weeks before the acute illness
ui.sepsis.cfs.name: Clinical Frailty Scale
ui.sepsis.cfs.note1: Grade the baseline state about two weeks before the acute illness, not how the patient looks during it.
ui.sepsis.cfs.note2: The scale was developed for people over 65; it does not apply to younger patients or to stable single-organ disability such as cerebral palsy.
ui.sepsis.cfs.note3: CFS ≥ 5 is widely taken as frailty and is associated with ICU mortality, prolonged stay and dependency after discharge.
ui.sepsis.cfs.note4: The score alone must not decide ICU admission or limitation of treatment; patient preferences and reversibility are weighed alongside it.
ui.sepsis.cfs.note5: Level 9 is for terminally ill patients with a life expectancy under six months, whatever their level of frailty.
ui.sepsis.cfs.option.l1: 1 · Very fit — robust, active, energetic; exercises regularly
ui.sepsis.cfs.option.l2: 2 · Fit — no active disease symptoms, exercises occasionally
ui.sepsis.cfs.option.l3: 3 · Managing well — medical problems controlled, not regularly active
ui.sepsis.cfs.option.l4: 4 · Living with very mild frailty — independent but slowed, tired during the day, symptoms starting to limit daily life
ui.sepsis.cfs.option.l5: 5 · Living with mild frailty — needs help with heavy housework, shopping, transport or medication
ui.sepsis.cfs.option.l6: 6 · Living with moderate frailty — needs help outside the home and on stairs, may need help bathing
ui.sepsis.cfs.option.l7: 7 · Living with severe frailty — completely dependent for personal care but stable, not at high risk of dying within months
ui.sepsis.cfs.option.l8: 8 · Living with very severe frailty — completely dependent, approaching the end of life, would not recover from a minor illness
ui.sepsis.cfs.option.l9: 9 · Terminally ill — life expectancy under 6 months, even if not otherwise evidently frail
ui.sepsis.cfs.reference: Rockwood K et al. CMAJ 2005;173:489-95; descriptors from version 2.0 (2020). ICU validity: Bagshaw SM et al. CMAJ 2014;186:E95-102.
ui.sepsis.cfs.subtitle: Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale · levels 1–9
ui.sepsis.cfs.summary: Grades frailty in nine levels based on the patient's baseline about two weeks before the acute illness. In the ICU a level of 5 or more is associated with poor outcome.
ui.sepsis.charlson.about: The Charlson comorbidity index was developed in 1987 to reduce the contribution of a patient's chronic conditions to long-term mortality into a single number. Charlson and colleagues followed 559 patients for a year, calculated how much each condition added to the risk of death, and assigned weights of 1, 2, 3 and 6 points according to relative risk: myocardial infarction, heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, dementia, chronic pulmonary disease, connective tissue disease, peptic ulcer, mild liver disease and uncomplicated diabetes score 1; diabetes with end-organ damage, hemiplegia, moderate to severe renal disease, leukemia, lymphoma and localized solid tumor score 2; moderate to severe liver disease scores 3; metastatic tumor and AIDS score 6. An age adjustment of 1 point per decade after 50 was added in 1994. In intensive care its value is that it shows the chronic reserve which APACHE II or SOFA, being measures of acute severity, cannot see: of two patients admitted with the same acute picture, the one carrying a heavy comorbidity burden is less likely to recover. It is also the most widely used comorbidity measure for comparing patient groups and adjusting for confounding in observational research.
ui.sepsis.charlson.band.b0.detail: No significant comorbidity. One-year mortality in the original cohort was about 12%.
ui.sepsis.charlson.band.b0.title: 0 points
ui.sepsis.charlson.band.b1.detail: Mild comorbidity burden. One-year mortality in the original cohort about 26%.
ui.sepsis.charlson.band.b1.title: 1–2 points
ui.sepsis.charlson.band.b3.detail: Moderate comorbidity burden. One-year mortality in the original cohort about 52%.
ui.sepsis.charlson.band.b3.title: 3–4 points
ui.sepsis.charlson.band.b5.detail: Heavy comorbidity burden. One-year mortality in the original cohort about 85%.
ui.sepsis.charlson.band.b5.title: 5 points or more
ui.sepsis.charlson.hint.age: Charlson 1994: 1 point for each decade over 40. This screen uses 50–59 → 1 · 60–69 → 2 · 70–79 → 3 · 80–89 → 4 · ≥ 90 → 5; some studies score ages 41–50 as 1 point
ui.sepsis.charlson.hint.aids: AIDS with a defining illness, not HIV positivity alone
ui.sepsis.charlson.hint.chf: Exertional dyspnea or heart failure responding to treatment
ui.sepsis.charlson.hint.connective: Rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus, polymyositis, polymyalgia rheumatica
ui.sepsis.charlson.hint.cvd: Transient ischemic attack or stroke with mild or no sequelae
ui.sepsis.charlson.hint.liver: Mild = cirrhosis without portal hypertension or chronic hepatitis; moderate to severe = portal hypertension, variceal bleeding
ui.sepsis.charlson.hint.pvd: Claudication, bypass, gangrene, untreated aortic aneurysm (≥ 6 cm)
ui.sepsis.charlson.hint.renal: Creatinine > 3 mg/dL, dialysis, transplantation or uremia
ui.sepsis.charlson.hint.tumor: Count tumors diagnosed within the past 5 years
ui.sepsis.charlson.name: Charlson comorbidity index
ui.sepsis.charlson.note1: The mortality figures come from Charlson's 1987 validation cohort of 685 patients and refer to one-year mortality; with modern treatment the absolute figures are lower.
ui.sepsis.charlson.note2: Mutually exclusive conditions are offered as single choices: only one level of diabetes, one severity of liver disease and one stage of tumor is scored.
ui.sepsis.charlson.note3: Metastatic solid tumor and AIDS are the heaviest items at 6 points; either alone moves the score into the high-risk band.
ui.sepsis.charlson.note4: The age adjustment was added in 1994; studies comparing disease burden alone may use the version without age.
ui.sepsis.charlson.note5: The index does not measure acute severity of illness; read it alongside an acute score such as APACHE II or SOFA when judging ICU outcome.
ui.sepsis.charlson.reference: Charlson ME et al. J Chronic Dis 1987;40:373-83. Age adjustment: Charlson ME et al. J Clin Epidemiol 1994;47:1245-51.
ui.sepsis.charlson.subtitle: Burden of comorbidity · age-adjusted
ui.sepsis.charlson.summary: Nineteen conditions are weighted by their contribution to mortality and points are added for age. Used to predict long-term mortality and to compare patient groups.
ui.sepsis.cpis.about: The Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score was described by Pugin and colleagues in 1991 to make the diagnosis of ventilator-associated pneumonia more objective. Temperature, white cell count, the amount and character of tracheal secretions, oxygenation, the infiltrate on the chest radiograph, progression of that infiltrate and tracheal aspirate culture are scored, giving a total of 0–12, with values above 6 suggesting pneumonia. It is usually applied in two stages: an initial assessment out of 10 before cultures return, then a recalculation on day 3 adding culture and radiographic progression. Its diagnostic performance is limited — against histological confirmation sensitivity and specificity sit around 65–70%, so it is not recommended as a stand-alone diagnostic criterion. Its practical value lies in serial measurement: a falling score on day 3 indicates response and gives confidence to shorten antibiotics, while a score that stays high calls for treatment to be reviewed. Because ARDS, atelectasis, pulmonary edema and contusion produce similar findings, a high score does not prove pneumonia.
ui.sepsis.cpis.band.high.detail: Together with the clinical picture this supports ventilator-associated pneumonia. Take a lower respiratory tract sample and start empirical treatment guided by local resistance.
ui.sepsis.cpis.band.high.title: 7 points or more · pneumonia likely
ui.sepsis.cpis.band.low.detail: Not enough support for ventilator-associated pneumonia. Look for alternative diagnoses and avoid unnecessary antibiotics.
ui.sepsis.cpis.band.low.title: 0–6 points · pneumonia unlikely
ui.sepsis.cpis.hint.culture: Add 1 point if the same organism is seen on Gram stain
ui.sepsis.cpis.hint.leukocytes: Add 1 point if band forms are ≥ 50%
ui.sepsis.cpis.hint.oxygenation: This item scores 0 in the presence of ARDS
ui.sepsis.cpis.hint.progression: Assessed after heart failure and ARDS have been excluded
ui.sepsis.cpis.hint.radiograph: Presence and distribution of the infiltrate
ui.sepsis.cpis.hint.secretions: Amount and character of secretions obtained on suctioning
ui.sepsis.cpis.hint.temperature: 36.5–38.4 °C → 0 points · 38.5–38.9 °C → 1 · ≥ 39 °C or ≤ 36.0 °C → 2. The range 36.1–36.4 °C, not defined in the source, scores 0 here
ui.sepsis.cpis.name: CPIS
ui.sepsis.cpis.note1: Pugin's original 1991 score has six items (0–12). In the modification by Singh et al. (2000) the first assessment uses five items without culture (0–10); progression of the infiltrate and culture are added on day 3. This screen adds all seven items, so the total can reach 14.
ui.sepsis.cpis.note2: Diagnostic accuracy is limited: systematic reviews report sensitivity and specificity around 65–70% against histological confirmation.
ui.sepsis.cpis.note3: Its main value is that a falling score on day 3 shows response to treatment and supports shortening antibiotics.
ui.sepsis.cpis.note4: ARDS, atelectasis, pulmonary edema, contusion and pulmonary embolism produce similar findings; consider the differential even when the score is high.
ui.sepsis.cpis.note5: The score does not replace the decision to start antibiotics; where pneumonia is suspected clinically, treatment should not be delayed once cultures are taken.
ui.sepsis.cpis.option.cultModerate: Moderate or heavy growth of a pathogen
ui.sepsis.cpis.option.cultModerateGram: Moderate to heavy growth with the same organism on Gram stain
ui.sepsis.cpis.reference: Pugin J et al. Am Rev Respir Dis 1991;143:1121-9. Modified version including progression of the infiltrate: Singh N et al. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2000;162:505-11.
ui.sepsis.cpis.subtitle: Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score · 7 items, 0–14 points
ui.sepsis.cpis.summary: Estimates the likelihood of ventilator-associated pneumonia from bedside findings, the chest radiograph and tracheal aspirate culture. A score above 6 suggests pneumonia.
ui.sepsis.cpot.about: CPOT is a behavioral scale developed to measure pain objectively in an intensive care patient who cannot describe it, because of intubation or clouded consciousness. Four domains are assessed: facial expression, body movements, muscle tension, and compliance with the ventilator in the intubated patient (vocalization in the extubated one). Each domain scores 0–2 for a total of 0–8, and a score above 2 is taken as significant pain. Its real strength lies not in a single value but in comparison: the difference between the score at rest and the score during a painful procedure such as turning or suctioning shows both that pain is present and whether analgesia is adequate. Vital signs such as heart rate and blood pressure are not reliable indicators of pain and should be treated only as a cue to look more carefully. Where the patient can self-report, their own rating always takes precedence over a behavioral scale.
ui.sepsis.cpot.band.high.detail: Review analgesia, pre-medicate before painful procedures and repeat the score afterwards to measure the response.
ui.sepsis.cpot.band.high.title: 3 points or more · pain present
ui.sepsis.cpot.band.low.detail: Current analgesia appears adequate. Repeat the measurement before and after procedures.
ui.sepsis.cpot.band.low.title: 0–2 points · no significant pain
ui.sepsis.cpot.hint.face: Observe at rest and during a painful procedure
ui.sepsis.cpot.hint.movements: Presence of movement, whether it is protective, and restlessness
ui.sepsis.cpot.hint.tension: Assessed by passive flexion and extension of the arm
ui.sepsis.cpot.hint.ventilator: Score ventilator compliance in the intubated patient and the sounds made in the extubated patient
ui.sepsis.cpot.item.ventilator: Compliance with the ventilator (intubated) or vocalization (extubated)
ui.sepsis.cpot.name: CPOT pain score
ui.sepsis.cpot.note1: Score separately at rest and during a painful procedure (turning, suctioning); the difference between the two guides treatment.
ui.sepsis.cpot.note2: The threshold is above 2: a score of 3 or more counts as significant pain.
ui.sepsis.cpot.note3: Do not use a behavioral scale in a patient who can self-report; the patient's own rating (NRS) takes precedence.
ui.sepsis.cpot.note4: Behavioural scales are unreliable under deep sedation and neuromuscular blockade, and vital sign changes alone are not a measure of pain.
ui.sepsis.cpot.note5: Agitation does not always mean pain; assess delirium (CAM-ICU) and sedation level (RASS) as well.
ui.sepsis.cpot.option.faceGrimacing: Grimacing — all of the above plus eyelids tightly closed
ui.sepsis.cpot.option.faceTense: Tense — frowning, brow lowering, orbit tightening
ui.sepsis.cpot.option.fighting: Fighting the ventilator · crying out, sobbing
ui.sepsis.cpot.option.protection: Protection — slow cautious movements, touching or rubbing the painful site
ui.sepsis.cpot.option.restlessness: Restlessness — pulling at tubes, trying to get out of bed, not following commands
ui.sepsis.cpot.option.tensionRelaxed: Relaxed — no resistance to passive movement
ui.sepsis.cpot.option.tensionTense: Tense, rigid — resistance to passive movement
ui.sepsis.cpot.option.tensionVeryTense: Very tense, rigid — strong resistance, movement cannot be completed
ui.sepsis.cpot.option.tolerating: Tolerating the ventilator · silent or talking in a normal tone
ui.sepsis.cpot.reference: Gélinas C et al. Am J Crit Care 2006;15:420-7. One of the two behavioral pain scales recommended in the SCCM PADIS 2018 guideline (the other is the BPS).
ui.sepsis.cpot.subtitle: Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool · 0–8 points
ui.sepsis.cpot.summary: Measures pain through behavior in the critically ill patient who cannot self-report. Four domains score 0–2; a total above 2 indicates significant pain.
ui.sepsis.dic.about: The ISTH overt DIC score is the algorithm published by Taylor and colleagues in 2001 to make the recognition of disseminated intravascular coagulation objective and reproducible. It applies only where an underlying disorder known to be associated with DIC is present — sepsis, trauma, obstetric complication, malignancy or severe liver disease, for example — and without that precondition the score is not valid. Platelet count, the rise in fibrin-related markers (D-dimer, fibrin degradation products), prolongation of the prothrombin time and fibrinogen level are scored; a total of 5 or more is compatible with overt DIC, and the score should be repeated daily. A total below 5 may suggest non-overt DIC and should be recalculated in 1–2 days. Its real function is to standardize the diagnosis; treatment is directed at the underlying cause, and decisions about blood products or anticoagulation are made separately according to bleeding, thrombosis or planned procedures.
ui.sepsis.dic.band.negative.detail: 0–4 points. DIC is not excluded; repeat within 1–2 days if suspicion persists.
ui.sepsis.dic.band.negative.title: No overt DIC
ui.sepsis.dic.band.positive.detail: 5 points or more is consistent with overt DIC. Treating the underlying cause is central; with bleeding, consider platelets, fresh frozen plasma and fibrinogen replacement.
ui.sepsis.dic.band.positive.title: Overt DIC
ui.sepsis.dic.name: ISTH overt DIC score
ui.sepsis.dic.note1: The score is valid only with a known underlying disorder (sepsis, trauma, malignancy, obstetric complication).
ui.sepsis.dic.note2: Repeat daily when positive and within 1–2 days when negative.
ui.sepsis.dic.note3: Fibrinogen is an acute phase reactant and can stay normal in sepsis, so it is misleading on its own.
ui.sepsis.dic.note4: D-dimer thresholds vary by laboratory; interpret against your own reference range.
ui.sepsis.dic.reference: Taylor FB et al., ISTH SSC; Thromb Haemost 2001;86:1327-30.
ui.sepsis.dic.subtitle: Disseminated intravascular coagulation · 0–8 points
ui.sepsis.dic.summary: Apply it only when an underlying disorder known to cause DIC is present. A total of 5 or more is consistent with overt DIC.
ui.sepsis.mews.about: MEWS is a bedside early warning score designed to catch clinical deterioration on the ward before cardiac arrest or an unplanned ICU admission. Systolic blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature and level of consciousness on the AVPU scale are each scored by how far they deviate from normal, giving a total of 0–14. In the 2001 validation by Subbe and colleagues in 709 medical admissions, a score of 5 or more was associated with a marked increase in death, ICU admission and high-dependency admission; that is why 5 is used in most protocols as the threshold for urgent medical review. Its strength is its simplicity and reproducibility: it needs no laboratory result, it is calculated straight from the nursing observation chart, and its real value lies not in a single reading but in the trend across consecutive readings. It is not diagnostic; it does not say which organ is failing, only how quickly the patient needs to be seen.
ui.sepsis.mews.band.high.detail: In the Subbe cohort a score of 5 or more was associated with death (OR 5.4) and ICU admission (OR 10.9). Arrange urgent medical review and consider critical care support.
ui.sepsis.mews.band.high.title: ≥ 5 points · high risk
ui.sepsis.mews.band.low.detail: Routine observation is enough; repeat the vital signs at the planned interval.
ui.sepsis.mews.band.low.title: 0–2 points · low risk
ui.sepsis.mews.band.moderate.detail: Increase the frequency of observation, inform the nurse in charge and the team, and reassess at a short interval.
ui.sepsis.mews.band.moderate.title: 3–4 points · moderate risk
ui.sepsis.mews.hint.avpu: Alert, responds to voice, responds to pain, unresponsive
ui.sepsis.mews.hint.systolic: ≤ 70 mmHg 3 points · 71–80 mmHg 2 · 81–100 mmHg 1 · 101–199 mmHg 0 · ≥ 200 mmHg 2
ui.sepsis.mews.name: MEWS score
ui.sepsis.mews.note1: The original Subbe 2001 version has five parameters; some hospital adaptations add hourly urine output. This screen uses the original version.
ui.sepsis.mews.note2: The maximum is 14 points. Reaching 3 points in a single parameter warrants review even when the total is low.
ui.sepsis.mews.note3: In the UK, MEWS has largely been replaced by NEWS2, which also covers oxygen saturation and supplemental oxygen. Stay with whichever your hospital uses.
ui.sepsis.mews.note4: Separate early warning systems exist for pregnancy, pediatrics and trauma (MEOWS, PEWS); this score is for the adult ward patient.
ui.sepsis.mews.reference: Subbe CP, Kruger M, Rutherford P, Gemmel L. Validation of a modified Early Warning Score in medical admissions. QJM 2001;94:521-6.
ui.sepsis.mews.subtitle: Modified Early Warning Score · 0–14 points
ui.sepsis.mews.summary: Five bedside parameters are scored. It was built to catch deterioration early on the ward; 5 points or more is high risk.
ui.sepsis.mnutric.about: NUTRIC (Nutrition Risk in the Critically Ill) is the first and only tool built specifically to assess nutrition risk in critical illness. What sets it apart is that it uses severity of illness, age, comorbidity and time spent in hospital before ICU admission rather than classical nutritional markers such as albumin, weight loss or body mass index — because the question it asks is not "is this patient malnourished" but "will this patient benefit from aggressive nutritional support". The modified version (mNUTRIC) drops interleukin-6, which is rarely measured in routine practice, making the score usable at the bedside; the total runs 0–9 and 5 or more is high risk. Reaching energy and protein targets has been reported to correlate with mortality in high-risk patients but not in low-risk ones, and that is precisely where the score earns its place: it shows where intensive feeding effort should be directed. Calculation requires APACHE II and SOFA, so it uses first-24-hour data, and feeding is not escalated aggressively until the patient is hemodynamically safe.
ui.sepsis.mnutric.band.high.detail: High nutrition risk; these are the patients most likely to benefit from early enteral feeding that reaches its target. Track calorie and protein delivery closely.
ui.sepsis.mnutric.band.high.title: 5–9 points · high risk
ui.sepsis.mnutric.band.low.detail: No additional benefit is expected from aggressive nutritional support. Follow the standard feeding protocol.
ui.sepsis.mnutric.band.low.title: 0–4 points · low risk
ui.sepsis.mnutric.hint.daysToICU: Same day (< 1 day) → 0 points · ≥ 1 day → 1 point
ui.sepsis.mnutric.item.daysToICU: Days from hospital to ICU admission
ui.sepsis.mnutric.name: mNUTRIC score
ui.sepsis.mnutric.note1: The modified version omits IL-6; the original NUTRIC including IL-6 runs 0–10 with a high-risk threshold of 6.
ui.sepsis.mnutric.note2: The score measures the likelihood of benefiting from nutritional support, not nutritional status; it contains no albumin, weight loss or body mass index.
ui.sepsis.mnutric.note3: Because it needs APACHE II and SOFA it is calculated from first-24-hour values.
ui.sepsis.mnutric.note4: Even in a high-risk patient, feeding should not be escalated aggressively until shock is controlled and the patient is hemodynamically safe.
ui.sepsis.mnutric.note5: The score alone is not a reason to start parenteral nutrition; the route is chosen according to current guidelines and whether the gut can be used.
ui.sepsis.mnutric.reference: Heyland DK et al. Crit Care 2011;15:R268 (NUTRIC). Modified version without IL-6: Rahman A et al. Clin Nutr 2016;35:158-62.
ui.sepsis.mnutric.subtitle: Modified NUTRIC nutrition risk · 0–9 points
ui.sepsis.mnutric.summary: Identifies the critically ill patients most likely to benefit from nutritional support. This is the modified version that does not need IL-6; 5 points or more is high risk.
ui.sepsis.news2.about: NEWS2 is the national early warning score published by the Royal College of Physicians in 2017 and adopted as the standard across the NHS. Respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, supplemental oxygen, systolic blood pressure, heart rate, level of consciousness and temperature are scored, giving a total of 0–20. It has two thresholds: 5–6 points is a medium-level alert calling for urgent review by a clinician, and 7 or more is a high-level alert calling for the emergency team. In addition, 3 points in any single parameter (a red score) warrants review in its own right even when the total is low. The main changes from the 2012 version are a second saturation scale with a target of 88–92% for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, and the addition of new-onset confusion to the consciousness item (CVPU). This screen implements Scale 1 only; Scale 2 should be used in hypercapnic patients such as those with COPD.
ui.sepsis.news2.band.high.detail: 7 points or more: continuous monitoring, emergency critical care review and consideration of a higher level of care.
ui.sepsis.news2.band.high.title: High risk
ui.sepsis.news2.band.low.detail: 1–4 points: observations at least every 4–6 hours; nursing review and medical notification if needed.
ui.sepsis.news2.band.low.title: Low risk
ui.sepsis.news2.band.medium.detail: 5–6 points (or 3 in any single parameter): hourly observations, urgent medical review and contact with the critical care team.
ui.sepsis.news2.band.medium.title: Medium risk
ui.sepsis.news2.band.routine.detail: 0 points: routine observations at least every 12 hours.
ui.sepsis.news2.band.routine.title: Routine monitoring
ui.sepsis.news2.hint.consciousness: New confusion or delirium counts as 'C'
ui.sepsis.news2.hint.spo2: Scale 2 is used in hypercapnic respiratory failure
ui.sepsis.news2.name: NEWS2
ui.sepsis.news2.note1: This screen uses Scale 1; in chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure (target SpO₂ 88–92%) Scale 2 applies.
ui.sepsis.news2.note2: Three points in any single parameter warrants urgent review even when the total is low.
ui.sepsis.news2.note3: The 2021 Surviving Sepsis guideline prefers tools such as NEWS over qSOFA for sepsis screening.
ui.sepsis.news2.note4: It is not valid in pregnancy or under 16 years of age; those groups use separate scores.
ui.sepsis.news2.reference: Royal College of Physicians, National Early Warning Score (NEWS) 2, 2017.
ui.sepsis.news2.subtitle: National Early Warning Score 2 · 0–20 points

ui.sepsis.prediliric.about: PRE-DELIRIC is a logistic regression model that predicts, within the first 24 hours of admission, how likely an intensive care patient is to develop delirium. It uses ten variables: age, APACHE II score, admission category, coma and its cause, infection, metabolic acidosis, morphine dose, use of sedatives, urea concentration and urgent admission. This screen applies the published shrunken regression coefficients exactly and reports the result as a percentage. The purpose is not diagnosis but identifying the high-risk patient before delirium appears, so that prevention can start early: early mobilization, protecting the sleep-wake cycle, providing glasses and hearing aids, reorientation, reducing noise and light, and minimizing sedation. The aim is to deliver that bundle in full to high-risk patients while not spending scarce resources on those at low risk. The model produces a probability; delirium itself should still be screened for every shift with CAM-ICU or ICDSC.

ui.sepsis.qsofa.about: qSOFA (quick SOFA) consists of the three criteria the Sepsis-3 task force defined so that a patient could be assessed at the bedside without waiting for laboratory results: respiratory rate ≥ 22/min, altered mentation and systolic blood pressure ≤ 100 mmHg. Outside the ICU, in patients with suspected infection, a score of 2 or more marks an increased risk of prolonged ICU stay and in-hospital death. It is not a diagnostic tool: specificity is high and sensitivity low, so a positive score strongly suggests a patient who may deteriorate, while a negative score does not rule out sepsis and must never delay cultures, antibiotics or fluids. Because of that limitation the Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 guideline recommends against using qSOFA as the single screening tool and prefers more sensitive early warning systems such as NEWS2. The mentation criterion is defined in the sources as GCS < 15 or GCS ≤ 13; this screen uses the ≤ 13 threshold.

ui.sepsis.qsofa.band.high.title: High risk
ui.sepsis.qsofa.band.low.detail: 0–1 points. A negative qSOFA does not rule out sepsis if clinical suspicion persists; check lactate and calculate SOFA.
ui.sepsis.qsofa.band.low.title: Low risk
ui.sepsis.qsofa.name: qSOFA
ui.sepsis.qsofa.note1: It is a screening tool: it is not diagnostic and does not by itself determine treatment.
ui.sepsis.qsofa.note2: The 2021 Surviving Sepsis guideline recommends against qSOFA as a single screening tool; NEWS or MEWS are preferred.
ui.sepsis.qsofa.note3: The altered mentation criterion is defined as GCS < 15 in some sources and GCS ≤ 13 in others; this screen uses the ≤ 13 threshold. Sensitivity is low and specificity high: a negative result does not exclude sepsis.
ui.sepsis.qsofa.note4: It was developed for settings outside the ICU (emergency department, wards).

ui.sepsis.sic.about: SIC (sepsis-induced coagulopathy) is a simplified score defined by the International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis in 2017 to capture the stage of coagulation disturbance in sepsis that precedes overt DIC. It has three components: platelet count, INR, and a SOFA subscore built from the respiratory, cardiovascular, hepatic and renal items, with the SOFA contribution capped at 2 points; a total of 4 or more meets the criteria for SIC. Compared with the overt DIC score it uses fewer variables, needs no fibrin degradation product, and turns positive earlier, which is why it has been used to select patients in anticoagulant trials. The score is not a diagnosis but a flag for the patient whose coagulation needs close monitoring; when it is positive, calculating the ISTH overt DIC score as well and prioritizing treatment of the underlying infection is recommended.
ui.sepsis.sic.band.negative.title: No SIC
ui.sepsis.sic.band.positive.detail: 4 points or more is consistent with sepsis-induced coagulopathy. Also calculate the ISTH DIC score for progression to overt DIC and weigh bleeding against thrombotic risk.
ui.sepsis.sic.band.positive.title: SIC present

ui.sepsis.sic.note2: The platelet and INR items each count a maximum of 2 points.
ui.sepsis.sic.note3: It has been used to select patients in anticoagulant trials; it is not by itself an indication for anticoagulation.
ui.sepsis.sic.note4: Liver disease and warfarin can make the INR item misleading.

ui.sepsis.sic.subtitle: Sepsis-induced coagulopathy · 0–6 points
ui.sepsis.sic.summary: Platelets, INR and a SOFA subscore. A total of 4 or more meets the SIC definition.
ui.sepsis.sofa.about: SOFA was developed at the 1994 consensus meeting of the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine to describe the degree and the course of organ dysfunction in the critically ill patient. Six systems are each scored 0–4: respiration (PaO₂/FiO₂), coagulation (platelets), liver (bilirubin), cardiovascular (mean arterial pressure and vasopressor requirement), central nervous system (GCS) and kidney (creatinine or urine output), giving a total of 0–24. The 2016 Sepsis-3 definition recast sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction, identified by an acute rise of 2 points or more in SOFA in a patient with suspected infection; where no organ failure is known, baseline SOFA is assumed to be zero. Septic shock is defined separately, by vasopressors being required to keep MAP ≥ 65 mmHg despite fluid resuscitation together with a lactate above 2 mmol/L. High and, above all, rising scores correlate strongly with mortality, but the score does not decide the fate of an individual patient: it describes and tracks the picture rather than prescribing treatment.

ui.sepsis.sofa.band.b0.title: 0–6 points
ui.sepsis.sofa.band.b10.title: 10–12 points
ui.sepsis.sofa.band.b13.title: 13–14 points
ui.sepsis.sofa.band.b15.detail: Mortality exceeds 80%; organ support and goals of care should be reassessed.
ui.sepsis.sofa.band.b15.title: 15 points or more
ui.sepsis.sofa.band.b7.title: 7–9 points

ui.sepsis.sofa.hint.respiration: mmHg; 3 and 4 points require respiratory support (mechanical ventilation or CPAP)

ui.sepsis.sofa.note1: Sepsis-3: suspected infection plus an acute rise of ≥2 SOFA points = sepsis.
ui.sepsis.sofa.note2: If chronic organ dysfunction is unknown, the baseline SOFA is taken as zero.
ui.sepsis.sofa.note3: Septic shock: vasopressor requirement to keep MAP ≥ 65 mmHg despite adequate fluid resuscitation, plus lactate > 2 mmol/L.
ui.sepsis.sofa.note4: Daily repeat scoring is more informative than a single reading; a rising SOFA is a poor prognostic sign.
