ui.sepsis.sofa2.about: SOFA-2 is the 2025 update of the SOFA score in use since 1996. It was developed and validated through a Delphi consensus involving sixty experts and data from 3.34 million patients in 1,319 ICUs across nine countries. Six organ systems (brain, respiratory, cardiovascular, liver, kidney, hemostasis) are still scored 0–4, but the thresholds were revised for contemporary intensive care: the respiratory component gained new cut-offs at 225 and 75 mmHg together with noninvasive support and ECMO, the cardiovascular component new catecholamine thresholds at 0.2 and 0.4 mcg/kg/min plus mechanical circulatory support, the kidney component hourly urine output and renal replacement therapy, and the brain component treatment for delirium. The largest changes are in the respiratory, kidney and cardiovascular components; liver and hemostasis only had their thresholds shifted. In the development study its discrimination for ICU mortality was better than the original SOFA, but how the Sepsis-3 rule of a 2-point rise performs with SOFA-2 is still being studied, so reading the two scores alongside each other remains the safest approach for now.
ui.sepsis.sofa2.band.b0.title: 0–1 points
ui.sepsis.sofa2.band.b12.detail: Severe multi-organ failure. Reassess goals of treatment and the level of organ support.
ui.sepsis.sofa2.band.b12.title: 12 points or more
ui.sepsis.sofa2.band.b2.detail: Mild to moderate organ dysfunction. In a patient with suspected infection an acute rise of 2 or more points from baseline meets the sepsis criterion.
ui.sepsis.sofa2.band.b2.title: 2–6 points
ui.sepsis.sofa2.band.b7.detail: Substantial multi-organ dysfunction; close monitoring and organ support are needed.
ui.sepsis.sofa2.band.b7.title: 7–11 points
ui.sepsis.sofa2.hint.brain: GCS; in the sedated patient use the response to command. Drug treatment for delirium scores 1 even with a GCS of 15
ui.sepsis.sofa2.hint.cardiovascular: Doses are the sum of norepinephrine and epinephrine (mcg/kg/min); other agent = vasopressin, dopamine, angiotensin II, dobutamine, levosimendan
ui.sepsis.sofa2.hint.kidney: Creatinine or urine output, whichever gives the higher score
ui.sepsis.sofa2.hint.respiration: PaO₂/FiO₂; advanced respiratory support = invasive ventilation, CPAP/BiPAP or high-flow nasal oxygen
ui.sepsis.sofa2.name: SOFA-2 score
ui.sepsis.sofa2.note1: SOFA-2 was developed on 3.34 million patients from 1,319 ICUs in nine countries and discriminated ICU mortality better than the original SOFA.
ui.sepsis.sofa2.note2: The Sepsis-3 rule of an acute rise of 2 or more points was defined with the original SOFA; how the same threshold behaves with SOFA-2 is still under validation.
ui.sepsis.sofa2.note3: This screen uses PaO₂/FiO₂ for the respiratory component. The source score also allows SpO₂/FiO₂ when no blood gas is available (SpO₂ must be ≤ 97%).
ui.sepsis.sofa2.note4: Drug treatment for delirium scores 1 point in the brain component even when the GCS is normal; this was not in the original SOFA.
ui.sepsis.sofa2.note5: In the kidney component a patient receiving or meeting criteria for renal replacement therapy — including chronic dialysis — scores 4.

ui.sepsis.sofa2.option.map70: MAP ≥ 70 mmHg, no vasopressor or inotrope
ui.sepsis.sofa2.option.mapUnder70: MAP < 70 mmHg, no vasopressor or inotrope

ui.sepsis.sofa2.option.rrt: Receiving or fulfilling criteria for renal replacement therapy

ui.sepsis.sofa2.summary: The 2025 update of the original SOFA. Thresholds were revised and noninvasive respiratory support, ECMO, mechanical circulatory support, renal replacement therapy and treated delirium were brought into the score.

ui.vaso.dexmedetomidine.note1: The FDA-approved ICU sedation dose is 0.2–0.7 mcg/kg/h (up to 24 hours); in practice it is used off-label up to 1.4 mcg/kg/h for deeper sedation or alcohol withdrawal.
ui.vaso.dexmedetomidine.note2: The loading dose (typically 0.5–1 mcg/kg over 10 minutes) is not calculated on this screen; only the maintenance infusion is calculated in mcg/kg/h.
ui.vaso.dexmedetomidine.note3: It is an α2-receptor agonist that provides sedation, anxiolysis and some analgesia without respiratory depression; patients remain easy to rouse.
ui.vaso.dexmedetomidine.note4: Skipping the loading dose or infusing it slowly lowers the incidence of bradycardia and hypotension.

ui.vaso.dexmedetomidine.warn1.message: Dose-dependent bradycardia and hypotension are common; monitor heart rate and blood pressure closely, especially during the loading dose.

ui.vaso.dexmedetomidine.warn2.message: The approved duration of use in the ICU is 24 hours; prolonged sedation protocols often exceed this.
ui.vaso.dexmedetomidine.warn2.title: FDA approval limited to 24 hours
ui.vaso.dexmedetomidine.warn3.message: Abrupt discontinuation after a prolonged infusion can cause rebound hypertension and tachycardia; taper gradually when possible.

ui.vaso.dobutamine.note1: Its predominant β1 effect increases cardiac output and contractility; systemic vascular resistance usually falls slightly or stays unchanged.
ui.vaso.dobutamine.note2: It is a first-line inotrope in cardiogenic shock and low-output heart failure; when hypotension is prominent it is combined with norepinephrine.
ui.vaso.dobutamine.note3: Tachyphylaxis can develop; effect may wane with continuous infusions beyond 72 hours.
ui.vaso.dobutamine.note4: Contraindicated in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, as it can worsen LVOT obstruction.

ui.vaso.dobutamine.warn2.message: Marked vasodilation can lower blood pressure; in hypotensive shock it is combined with norepinephrine.
ui.vaso.dobutamine.warn2.title: Insufficient alone in hypotensive patients
ui.vaso.dobutamine.warn3.message: Abrupt discontinuation after a prolonged infusion can cause haemodynamic deterioration; taper gradually when possible.
ui.vaso.dobutamine.warn3.title: Do not stop abruptly

ui.vaso.dopamine.band.alpha.title: α dose
ui.vaso.dopamine.band.beta.detail: 3–10 mcg/kg/min: inotropic effect; cardiac output and heart rate rise.
ui.vaso.dopamine.band.beta.title: β dose
ui.vaso.dopamine.band.dopaminergic.detail: 1–3 mcg/kg/min: no proven clinical benefit; routine use is not recommended.
ui.vaso.dopamine.band.dopaminergic.title: Dopaminergic dose
ui.vaso.dopamine.band.excessive.detail: Above 20 mcg/kg/min adds no benefit; switch to an alternative vasopressor.
ui.vaso.dopamine.band.excessive.title: Excessive dose
ui.vaso.dopamine.name: Dopamine
ui.vaso.dopamine.note1: As the dose rises, dopaminergic, then β, then α receptor effects come to the fore.
ui.vaso.dopamine.note2: In septic shock it causes more arrhythmia than norepinephrine and is a second-line agent in current guidelines.
ui.vaso.dopamine.note3: It may be preferred in bradycardic patients at low risk of arrhythmia.
ui.vaso.dopamine.note4: Low-dose dopamine has no proven renal protective effect; the concept of a renal dose has been abandoned.

ui.vaso.dopamine.warn2.message: Tachyarrhythmias are markedly more frequent than with norepinephrine; continuous ECG monitoring is required.
ui.vaso.dopamine.warn2.title: Arrhythmia risk
ui.vaso.dopamine.warn3.message: Norepinephrine is first line in septic shock; keep dopamine for selected patients.
ui.vaso.dopamine.warn3.title: Guideline position

ui.vaso.norepinephrine.band.low.detail: 0.01–0.05 mcg/kg/min: the starting range. Volume status should be reassessed.
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.band.low.title: Low dose
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.band.moderate.detail: 0.05–0.3 mcg/kg/min: the range used most often in septic shock.
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.band.moderate.title: Moderate dose
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.band.veryHigh.detail: Above 1 mcg/kg/min: refractory shock. Look for acidosis, hypocalcemia, adrenal insufficiency and mechanical causes.
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.band.veryHigh.title: Very high dose
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.name: Norepinephrine
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.note1: In septic shock the usual mean arterial pressure target is ≥ 65 mmHg; titrate the dose to that target.
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.note2: Weight-based dosing (mcg/kg/min) is common, but some units use a fixed mcg/min. Make the unit explicit at handover.
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.note3: Raising the dose before correcting hypovolemia worsens tissue perfusion; assess fluid responsiveness.
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.note4: Above 0.25–0.5 mcg/kg/min, adding vasopressin can reduce the norepinephrine requirement.
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.tagline: α₁-dominant vasopressor · first line in septic shock
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.warn1.message: It is a potent vasoconstrictor and is preferably given through a central line. If a peripheral line is unavoidable use a large vein for a short time with close observation; consider phentolamine infiltration for extravasation.
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.warn1.title: Risk of extravasation
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.warn2.message: Watch for tachyarrhythmia and end-organ or mesenteric ischemia; judge the response with lactate, urine output and capillary refill.
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.warn2.title: Monitor rhythm and perfusion
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.warn3.message: Abrupt discontinuation causes severe hypotension; taper gradually and reassess volume status at the same time.
ui.vaso.norepinephrine.warn3.title: When weaning

ui.vaso.vasopressin.name: Vasopressin
ui.vaso.vasopressin.note1: In septic shock it is added to norepinephrine at a fixed 0.03 units/min; titration is not recommended.
ui.vaso.vasopressin.note2: It acts through a different receptor from the catecholamines and keeps its effect in acidosis.
ui.vaso.vasopressin.note3: It is usually started at 0.01 units/min and increased to 0.03 units/min.
ui.vaso.vasopressin.note4: Which agent is weaned first varies by unit protocol; abrupt discontinuation can cause hypotension.

ui.vaso.vasopressin.warn1.message: Digital, mesenteric and coronary ischemia can occur at higher doses; exceeding 0.04 units/min is not recommended.

indications.title: Barbiturate coma
indications.subtitle: Refractory intracranial hypertension
indications.target: Burst suppression on EEG (3–8 s of suppression) and ICP < 20 mmHg
notes: The loading dose is usually given as divided boluses (e.g. 5 mg/kg, then 1–2 mg/kg over 1–2 hours).
Hypotension is expected; have vasopressors and invasive arterial monitoring ready.
Taper gradually when stopping; abrupt discontinuation can cause rebound intracranial hypertension.

indications.title: Refractory status epilepticus
indications.subtitle: Seizures unresponsive to other agents
indications.target: Seizure suppression or burst suppression on EEG
notes: Intubation, mechanical ventilation and continuous EEG monitoring are mandatory.
Continue for 24–48 hours after seizure control, then taper gradually.

indications.title: Anesthesia maintenance
indications.subtitle: TIVA maintenance after induction
indications.target: Clinical depth of anesthesia with BIS 40–60
notes: Maintenance with thiopental is rare today; emergence is markedly delayed in longer cases.
If the case exceeds 1–2 hours, consider switching to propofol or an inhalational agent.

indications.title: Sedation / maintenance
indications.subtitle: Low-dose sedation in intensive care
indications.target: Target sedation score (RASS) and hemodynamic stability
notes: It accumulates in tissue during long infusions; emergence can take hours to days after stopping.
Plan a daily sedation hold and neurological assessment.

standingWarnings.title: Incompatibility: flush the line
standingWarnings.message: Thiopental is strongly alkaline (pH ≈ 10.5). It precipitates with acidic drugs such as succinylcholine, rocuronium, vecuronium, atracurium, midazolam and ondansetron. Flush with normal saline before and after any drug given through the same line, and use a separate lumen when possible.

standingWarnings.title: Contraindications
standingWarnings.message: Acute intermittent porphyria and its variants, hypersensitivity to thiobarbiturates, any situation where the airway cannot be secured, decompensated heart failure or severe hypovolemia (relative).

cumulative24h.title: High cumulative dose
cumulative24h.message: {mg} mg ({g} g) over 24 hours. Thiopental shifts to zero-order kinetics during long infusions; emergence can take days after stopping. Consider reducing the daily dose and titrating to EEG.

limitMessages.peripheral: Solutions above 2.5% (25 mg/mL) increase venous irritation and the risk of tissue necrosis on extravasation. For continuous infusion prefer a central line or a more dilute solution.
limitMessages.maximum: Solutions above 5% (50 mg/mL) are not recommended for thiopental; check the preparation.

pharmacology: 3–12 hours; markedly prolonged after long infusions
Hepatic; zero-order kinetics at high doses
adverseEffects: Dose-dependent myocardial depression and venodilation → hypotension
Respiratory depression and apnea; a secured airway is mandatory
Reduction in cerebral blood flow, cerebral metabolic rate and intracranial pressure
Laryngospasm and bronchospasm at light planes of anesthesia
Histamine release, urticaria, rarely anaphylaxis
Severe vasospasm and tissue necrosis after intra-arterial injection
Tissue accumulation, delayed emergence, ileus and infection risk during long infusions
contraindications: Acute intermittent porphyria and its variants
reference.incompatibilityNote: Thiopental is strongly alkaline; mixing with acidic drugs forms a precipitate that can occlude the line. Flush with normal saline before and after every administration.
reference.preparationNote: The lyophilized powder is reconstituted with sterile water or 0.9% sodium chloride. The solution must be clear; discard it if cloudy or if a precipitate is present. Use the prepared solution within 24 hours at room temperature (per institutional protocol).
practicalTips: On extravasation stop the injection, leave the cannula in place and aspirate.
After intra-arterial injection keep the catheter in place and consult the relevant specialty for a local vasodilator and heparinization.
Elevate the limb, provide analgesia and request a plastic surgery consultation.
Record the event and its time in the patient's chart.

indications.title: Anesthesia maintenance (TIVA)
indications.subtitle: Maintenance infusion after induction
indications.target: Clinical depth of anesthesia with BIS 40–60; balanced titration with an opioid
notes: It is common practice to start near the upper limit (133–167 mcg/kg/min; 8–10 mg/kg/h) for the first 10–15 minutes and then reduce stepwise.
50 mcg/kg/min = 3 mg/kg/h; 200 mcg/kg/min = 12 mg/kg/h.
Propofol requirements fall markedly when an opioid (remifentanil/fentanyl) is co-administered.
Emergence is usually 5–10 minutes after stopping; the context-sensitive half-time lengthens in long cases.
monitoring: Arterial pressure (hypotension is common at induction)
Triglycerides and lactate in long cases

standingWarnings.title: Infection control
standingWarnings.message: The lipid emulsion supports microbial growth. Draw the drug immediately after opening the ampoule or vial and change the syringe and giving set at least every 12 hours (6–12 hours per institutional protocol). Strict aseptic technique is mandatory.

standingWarnings.title: Injection pain
standingWarnings.message: Burning in a peripheral vein is common. A large vein, or 20–40 mg of lidocaine or an opioid given before propofol, reduces the pain.

standingWarnings.title: Contraindications and cautions
standingWarnings.message: Hypersensitivity to propofol or its components (soy, peanut, egg lecithin). The risk of hypotension is pronounced in severe hypovolemia, low ejection fraction and in the elderly; reduce the dose. Use with caution in severe disorders of fat metabolism.

pris.title: PRIS risk: dose above 67 mcg/kg/min (4 mg/kg/h)
pris.message: Propofol infusion syndrome is associated with doses above 4 mg/kg/h (≈ 67 mcg/kg/min) continued beyond 48 hours (metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, cardiac failure). In the operating room {dose} mcg/kg/min is ordinary for short maintenance; in prolonged cases lower the dose with opioid or inhalational support and monitor lactate, CK and triglycerides.

lipidLoad.title: Lipid and calorie load
lipidLoad.message: At this rate 24 hours deliver {ml} mL of {percent}% emulsion ≈ {fat} g of fat / {kcal} kcal. Include it in the nutrition plan and monitor triglycerides during prolonged infusions.

obesityDosingWeight.title: Obesity: use adjusted weight for maintenance
obesityDosingWeight.message: Propofol induction is dosed on lean body weight, while the maintenance infusion is usually based on adjusted body weight. Maintenance on total body weight can lead to overdosing (ABW {adjusted} kg).

limitMessages.maximum: The commercial formulations are 1% (10 mg/mL) and 2% (20 mg/mL). Propofol is normally used undiluted; if dilution is required use 5% dextrose only and do not go below 2 mg/mL.

pharmacology: ~10 min after a 1-hour infusion; ~40 min after 8 hours
Antiemetic effect, reduced cerebral metabolic rate, bronchodilation
adverseEffects: Dose-dependent hypotension (vasodilation plus myocardial depression)
Apnea and respiratory depression; airway support required
Pain and burning at the injection site
Bradycardia, especially with opioids
Propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS) with prolonged high doses
Hypertriglyceridemia and pancreatitis during long infusions
Green discoloration of urine (harmless)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to propofol, soy, peanut or egg components
Severe hypovolemia or shock (relative; requires dose reduction)
incompatibilities: Mixing with neuromuscular blockers in the same line
Same lumen as blood or blood products
reference.incompatibilityNote: Give propofol through a separate line or a well-flushed lumen; discard the solution if the emulsion separates into phases.
reference.preparationNote: Normally used undiluted. Shake the ampoule or vial before use; the emulsion must be homogeneous and milky white. Discard any product showing phase separation.
practicalTips: Maintaining the upper dose for 10 minutes after induction and then stepping down makes titration easier.
Combined with remifentanil, propofol requirements fall by roughly one third.
Reduce the dose 5–10 minutes before the end of surgery to speed emergence.
Label the syringe pump with the drug name and concentration; confusing 1% with 2% causes serious dosing errors.

indications.title: Intraoperative analgesia
indications.subtitle: Maintenance analgesia during general anesthesia
indications.target: Suppression of the hemodynamic response to surgical stimulation (less than 20% change in heart rate and arterial pressure)
notes: Dose on lean or ideal body weight; using total body weight overdoses the obese patient.
It does not accumulate: the context-sensitive half-time stays 3–5 minutes regardless of infusion duration.
If a bolus is needed, give it slowly over 30–60 seconds; a rapid bolus causes chest wall rigidity and bradycardia.
Plan a longer-acting analgesic (morphine, paracetamol, NSAID, regional block) before the infusion is stopped.
monitoring: Depth of anesthesia — it does not produce unconsciousness on its own

standingWarnings.title: Plan analgesia before stopping
standingWarnings.message: The effect disappears completely 5–10 minutes after the infusion stops; sudden severe pain and opioid-induced hyperalgesia can follow. Give a longer-acting analgesic or a regional block before the infusion ends.

standingWarnings.title: It does not produce unconsciousness
standingWarnings.message: Remifentanil is an analgesic opioid; it must be combined with propofol or an inhalational agent for hypnosis. Used alone it carries a risk of awareness.

standingWarnings.title: Contraindications
standingWarnings.message: Hypersensitivity to fentanyl derivatives. Because the formulation contains glycine, epidural and intrathecal use is contraindicated. Make sure the preparation is given intravenously only.

obesityLeanWeight.title: Obesity: do not use total body weight
obesityLeanWeight.message: Remifentanil is dosed on lean ({lean} kg) or ideal ({ideal} kg) body weight. Using total body weight ({total} kg) creates a serious risk of respiratory depression and bradycardia.

slowBolus.title: Give the bolus slowly
slowBolus.message: A bolus of {bolus} mcg/kg must be given over at least 30–60 seconds. Rapid injection can cause chest wall rigidity, apnea, bradycardia and hypotension; keep a neuromuscular blocker and atropine at hand.

highDose.title: High analgesic dose
highDose.message: Bradycardia and hypotension become more frequent at 0.3 mcg/kg/min and above. Review the hypnotic dose as well; propofol requirements usually fall.

limitMessages.maximum: The recommended working concentration is 20–50 mcg/mL (250 mcg/mL maximum). In a more concentrated solution small rate errors translate into large dose differences.

pharmacology: Similar to fentanyl, with a far shorter effect
doses: Effect ends 5–10 min after the infusion stops
adverseEffects: Bradycardia and hypotension (dose dependent)
Respiratory depression and apnea
Chest wall and glottic rigidity after a rapid bolus
Acute pain and opioid-induced hyperalgesia after discontinuation
Nausea, vomiting, pruritus
Difficult mask ventilation due to muscle rigidity
contraindications: Any setting without airway and ventilatory support
incompatibilities: Same lumen as blood or blood products
reference.incompatibilityNote: Do not run it in the same line as alkaline drugs such as thiopental. Remifentanil left in the tubing can be delivered as an unintended bolus when the rate changes; use a separate lumen with minimal dead space.
reference.preparationNote: Reconstitute the vial to 1 mg per mL, then dilute to 20–50 mcg/mL with 0.9% sodium chloride or 5% dextrose. Use the prepared solution within 24 hours.
practicalTips: Start the infusion before the surgical stimulus; both onset and offset are fast.
Connect the pump line to the port closest to the patient; drug left in a long line causes unwanted boluses.
Always establish longer-acting analgesia before extubation.
0.1 mcg/kg/min = 6 mcg/kg/h; in a 70 kg patient with a 50 mcg/mL solution that is 8.4 mL/h.

indications.title: Anesthesia maintenance
indications.subtitle: Maintenance infusion after induction
indications.target: Clinical depth of anesthesia with hemodynamic stability and adequate analgesia
notes: 1–3 mg/kg/h ≈ 17–50 mcg/kg/min. Analgesic (sub-anesthetic) doses are far lower: 0.1–0.5 mg/kg/h.
It is usually combined with a benzodiazepine or propofol; emergence reactions are common when used alone.
It increases secretions; consider an antisialagogue such as atropine or glycopyrrolate.
Reducing the dose 15–30 minutes before the end of surgery smooths emergence.
monitoring: Depth of anesthesia — BIS is less reliable with ketamine

standingWarnings.title: Emergence reaction
standingWarnings.message: Vivid dreams, hallucinations and delirium can occur. Co-administered midazolam reduces the incidence; provide a quiet, low-stimulus recovery area.

standingWarnings.title: Sympathomimetic effect
standingWarnings.message: It raises heart rate, arterial pressure and myocardial oxygen consumption. Use with caution in severe coronary artery disease, uncontrolled hypertension, aortic aneurysm and severe pulmonary hypertension. In catecholamine-depleted patients it can instead cause myocardial depression.

standingWarnings.title: Contraindications
standingWarnings.message: Hypersensitivity to ketamine. It is relatively contraindicated in selected patients with uncontrolled hypertension, acute coronary syndrome or raised intracranial or intraocular pressure. Exacerbation has been reported in patients with schizophrenia.

highMaintenance.title: High maintenance dose
highMaintenance.message: {dose} mg/kg/h is at the top of the range for anesthesia maintenance. Emergence reactions, increased secretions and delayed awakening become more frequent; consider benzodiazepine support and a dose reduction.

undiluted.title: Undiluted solution
undiluted.message: Infusing 50 mg/mL directly requires very small rates ({rate} mL/h). Dilute to 5–10 mg/mL to reduce dosing error.

obesityDosingWeight.title: Obesity: dosing weight
obesityDosingWeight.message: Ketamine is lipophilic; for prolonged infusions in obesity prefer lean ({lean} kg) or adjusted ({adjusted} kg) body weight.

limitMessages.maximum: The commercial vial is at most 50 mg/mL. Diluting to 1–10 mg/mL for continuous infusion reduces dosing error.

pharmacology: Largely preserves respiration and airway reflexes
adverseEffects: Tachycardia, hypertension and increased myocardial oxygen consumption
Emergence reaction: hallucinations, vivid dreams, agitation
Increased salivary and bronchial secretions
Nystagmus, diplopia, raised intraocular pressure
Nausea and vomiting
Increased muscle tone and involuntary movements
Tolerance, raised liver enzymes and urinary symptoms with prolonged use
contraindications: Raised intraocular pressure, penetrating eye injury (relative)
reference.incompatibilityNote: Ketamine is an acidic solution; it precipitates with alkaline drugs such as thiopental in the same line. Use a separate lumen or flush the line.
reference.preparationNote: Dilute the 50 mg/mL vial with 0.9% sodium chloride or 5% dextrose. For continuous infusion 1–10 mg/mL is the practical range; always state the concentration on the syringe label.
practicalTips: Co-administered midazolam or propofol markedly reduces emergence reactions.
It is the maintenance agent of choice in the hemodynamically unstable, hypovolemic or bronchospastic patient.
An antisialagogue reduces secretions and improves airway safety.
A low-dose adjunct infusion (0.1–0.3 mg/kg/h) can be planned to reduce opioid consumption.
